ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial academic tone, with mostly medium-to-long turns during presentations and short, often fragmented exchanges before and after them. Overlap and interruptions are light but common in the informal chat, while the Q&A is orderly, with speakers usually waiting to be acknowledged. Participants use frequent fillers and repairs—“um,” “yeah,” “right,” repeated words, false starts, and self-corrections—giving the speech an unrehearsed video-call feel. Questions tend to begin with praise or hedging (“great talk,” “I have a naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then develop into multi-part exploratory prompts. Responses are generous and speculative, often framing uncertainty explicitly with phrases like “I think,” “we haven’t looked at that,” “it could be,” and “I don’t know.” Challenges are indirect and collaborative: people raise alternative interpretations or limitations as open questions rather than objections, and speakers validate the question before qualifying their answer. Introductions and transitions are somewhat formal, but the overall interaction remains warm, lightly joking, and conversational.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.

  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Judging whether a headband neurofeedback program improves attention in elementary classrooms.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Associate professor of cognitive neuroscience with 14 years of experience studying attention development and EEG-based self-regulation in children. She has led laboratory and school-partnership studies using EEG spectral features, event-related measures, and longitudinal behavioral follow-up, and regularly collaborates with clinicians and educators on translating neural measures into functional outcomes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats EEG attention markers as mechanistic or proximal indicators rather than evidence of educational value in themselves. She will press the group to distinguish changes in neural signal or trained task performance from meaningful improvements in classroom attention and learning, consider placebo and expectation-related effects, and include a post-program follow-up to test whether any gains persist. She is comfortable specifying neurophysiological measures but defers to education colleagues on which classroom outcomes are consequential and to engineering colleagues on device performance limits.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Romero
speakers.background: Doctoral candidate in educational psychology with 6 years of experience as an elementary classroom teacher and district-based research coordinator. His work examines classroom engagement, teacher-rated attention, instructional time, and implementation of school interventions across resource-diverse schools. He has conducted teacher interviews, classroom observations, mixed-methods feasibility studies, and curriculum-aligned learning assessments.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis defines success in terms of classroom-relevant attention and learning, not improvement on a device or a laboratory-style attention measure. He will ask whether individual sessions displace instruction, whether teachers view the workflow as workable, and whether educators will buy into implementation. He will insist on an equity plan that prevents access from depending on a school's staffing, quiet-space availability, device capacity, or a student's comfort with wearables, and he will advocate for teacher feedback and implementation records alongside outcome measures.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Priya Nair
speakers.background: Research engineer with 9 years of experience developing and field-testing wearable biosensing systems, including dry-electrode EEG headbands used with children and adolescents. Her work includes bench testing, battery and connectivity validation, human-factors assessment, safety documentation, fit procedures, signal-quality monitoring, and troubleshooting deployments in nonlaboratory settings.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya views the device as part of the intervention rather than a neutral measurement tool. She will emphasize that dry-electrode contact quality, child-specific fit, movement artifacts, battery reliability, device safety, and tolerance of the headband can determine both whether neurofeedback is delivered as intended and whether EEG data can be interpreted. She will press for systematic technical and implementation logs, safety reports, fit and signal-quality checks, and realistic procedures for schools with different infrastructure, while challenging outcome plans that assume all recorded EEG is equally valid.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary research discussion with an identifiable research problem. The evaluated AI must summarize the whole discussion and acknowledge the participating disciplines.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning discussion among all three participants. Dr. Chen should explain that improved EEG-based attention markers alone would not establish meaningful classroom benefit, raise placebo/expectation effects, and request a follow-up measure after the program ends to assess durability. Dr. Romero should define the educational concern as whether the program improves classroom-relevant attention and learning without unacceptable loss of instructional time, ask for teacher feasibility and buy-in measures, and require an equity plan so access is not limited by school resources or student characteristics. Nair should explain that dry-electrode signal quality, child-specific headband fit, device safety, and battery reliability can affect both whether the intervention works and whether EEG data are interpretable; she should propose recording these implementation and technical measures. The group should converge on a shared research problem: determining whether a feasible, safe, and equitably delivered 10-week headband neurofeedback program produces durable improvements in elementary students' classroom attention and learning, beyond expectation-related effects, while maintaining acceptable classroom disruption. They should discuss a comparison condition that matches adult attention and device-related expectations, but leave the exact comparison protocol unresolved pending district approval. They should agree that the proposal will combine classroom attention observations or teacher ratings, a learning outcome aligned to participating classrooms, EEG data-quality/attention-marker measures, implementation records, safety reports, teacher feedback, and a post-program follow-up. Do not resolve the exact sample size, final attention instrument, final learning assessment, or exact follow-up interval.

ground_truth.summary: The team formulates an interdisciplinary pilot-study problem: assess whether a 10-week classroom neurofeedback headband program can safely, feasibly, and equitably yield durable improvements in elementary students' real classroom attention and learning, rather than merely changes in EEG markers or expectation-driven effects. The discussion recognizes that technical performance and classroom implementation are part of the causal and evaluative problem, not peripheral details.

neuroscience: EEG attention markers are not sufficient evidence of educational benefit.
Expectation/placebo effects require an expectation-matched comparison condition.
Outcomes should include a post-program follow-up to test durability.
education: Primary outcomes must be classroom-relevant attention and learning.
The study must measure lesson-time disruption, teacher feasibility, and teacher buy-in.
Equity requires attention to unequal school resources and students' ability to access or tolerate the program.
biomedical_engineering: Dry-electrode signal quality and child-specific fit affect data validity and intervention delivery.
Safety and battery reliability must be monitored.
Technical failures and usability measures should be recorded as implementation data.

agreed_design_elements: A 10-week pilot in grades 3-5 across four elementary schools.
An expectation- and attention-matched comparison condition in principle, with its exact protocol still unresolved.

Combined outcomes: classroom attention observation or teacher ratings; a classroom-aligned learning outcome; EEG marker and signal-quality data; device fit, battery, and technical-failure records; safety reports; teacher feedback; and implementation/lesson-time records.
A post-program follow-up to evaluate durability.
An equity plan addressing differing school resources, access to quiet space, device availability, and student tolerance of wearable equipment.
ground_truth.key_decision: The proposal should not claim success based solely on EEG changes; it should evaluate educational benefit, expectation effects, durability, implementation burden, equity, and device performance together.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Before we get too far into the proposal mechanics, I was hoping today we could get clear on what would actually count as a meaningful attention outcome in the classroom, not just a nicer EEG trace or better performance during feedback. I guess, across the four schools, then we can work backward to what’s feasible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: For the district, it has to show up during ordinary instruction, teacher-rated on-task behavior, maybe a brief classroom observation measure, and some learning indicator tied to what that grade is actually covering. And I'd want us to count the cost too, minutes out of class, missed sessions, and whether teachers can keep the workflow going on a busy...

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Those are the right outcomes, but I don't think we should treat the headband data as a clean secondary measure by default. For each session, we need a fit and signal-quality check, along with battery, connection, and interruption logs. Otherwise, a child who's uncomfortable or moving may look like they got the same intervention when they really didn't. Luis, what would teachers see as a realistic way to record the actual minutes out of instruction?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I'd keep it very low burden. Just a session start and end time, plus a simple reason code if it doesn't happen, like testing, transition, staffing, student declined, that sort of thing. The intervention staff should probably enter most of that, rather than asking classroom teachers to reconstruct it later. Then we'd have a very brief weekly teacher check on whether it disrupted instruction more broadly.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That seems workable. I’d add a short technician-entered reason code for sessions that start but can’t yield usable feedback—poor contact, repeated motion, connection loss, or a child asking to stop—because those are different from an ordinary missed session. Otherwise the attendance record could make delivery look much more consistent—more complete than it really was.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, and child-initiated stops.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: And I’d treat those as important data, not just an implementation nuisance. If child-initiated stops cluster at one school, or for particular students, then an average outcome could hide that the program was really, really only accessible to a subset of children.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Yes. We should distinguish a child choosing to stop because the band is uncomfortable from a stop after repeated poor-signal prompts or a device fault. Those can look similar in a simple log, but they imply different changes to the protocol. I have seen signal quality deteriorate only after several wears for a few children, so I would want the fit and comfort check recorded at every session, not just at enrollment. And the- actually, that needs to be recorded every session, not just at enrollment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Hm, every session, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think every session is important, particularly because those comfort and signal problems could otherwise get folded into an apparent nonresponse. Priya, do you have a sense of whether a very brief child comfort rating before or after each session would be interpretable alongside the fit log, or, or does that become too much for grades 3 through 5?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: A very short rating could work if it's concrete. Maybe a three-face scale for comfort after the session, and they could say they want to stop or don't want to wear it again. I wouldn't treat it as a precise measure, but alongside the technician's fit notes and whether the child moved or stopped, it would help us tell- it would help us distinguish discomfort from a purely technical contact problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That seems proportionate. For the 10-week pilot, I’d want to see whether comfort ratings and usable-signal rates change over the weeks, not just look at the overall average. Initial novelty or irritation could look very different from something that persists. And it helps us avoid treating the kids who quietly stop tolerating it as ordinary missing data.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Right, over time too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: And I think we should look at whether those patterns differ by school, not just by week. If the school with the least private space has more stops or lower usable sessions, that's not really a child-level tolerance finding. It's telling us something about the delivery conditions. We'd need teacher input on that too, because a child may rate the band fine but still be, be reluctant to leave during a particular lesson.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That matters for interpreting any neural change too. A quieter, more predictable pull-out context could affect state regulation, or even just the child’s expectation of the session, so I’d be hesitant to pool schools as though delivery were interchangeable. Luis, for the classroom outcome, could the observation window be anchored to the lesson they would otherwise have missed, or the- would that be too disruptive?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: It could work if it’s a naturally occurring instructional block, instead of adding an observation just because of the study. But I’d be careful calling it the lesson they “would otherwise have missed,” because schedules shift and the pull-out may fall in different subjects across schools. We could record the subject and lesson type for each session, then sample classroom attention in a common window, maybe the same core block, if teachers say that’s realistic.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That makes sense. I’d want the session record to capture the subject and the location too, because a noisy hallway or an improvised corner could change motion and contact quality even if the scheduled block is the same. We should probably ask each school what quiet space is actually, actually available when we’d run the sessions, instead of assuming the room listed on paper is usable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm-hm. And for me, the setting isn't just an implementation covariate. It may alter arousal and expectancy enough to change the proximal EEG measures. I'd want to know from each school, before we choose any EEG outcome, whether that space is actually consistent session to session, or whether children are sometimes, sometimes in a hallway, sometimes in a resource room, because those are pretty different recording contexts.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: And I’d add that we need to record the actual location for every session, not just the school’s planned room. A stable room can still have a fire drill, a shared-space interruption, or poor Wi-Fi that changes the feedback workflow. Before we settle on an EEG endpoint, Maya, what minimum quality information would you need to regard a session’s attention- attention marker as interpretable?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d need the raw- or at least I’d want the signal-quality metrics retained, along with an electrode-contact or impedance proxy if the device provides one, the proportion of artifact-free epochs, and a clear flag for whether feedback was actually delivered for most of the session. I wouldn’t set a universal threshold until we see the vendor’s outputs and a few field recordings, though. With dry electrodes in children, a session can look nominally complete but have really uneven usable data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Yeah, that seems right.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I agree, we shouldn't fix thresholds yet. We should also retain enough of the device status record to distinguish a low-quality recording from feedback that was degraded in real time. Those aren't necessarily the same thing. I need to check what this particular vendor actually exposes, including the contact metric and raw-data, I mean raw-data access, before we promise an EEG endpoint in the proposal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That vendor check is pretty central, because I'd rather frame the neural piece as an exploratory proximal measure than promise a biomarker endpoint we can't audit. For the study question, the actual study question, I think we should ask whether the program is feasible and acceptable across these delivery contexts, and whether any classroom on-task change is still there after the ten weeks, maybe with a short post-program follow-up if Luis thinks the teacher burden is tolerable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: A short follow-up is worth trying, but I'd need to check the assessment calendar and pacing with the schools before we promise a learning measure at that point. For the proposal, could we frame the primary question as feasibility, acceptability, and equitable delivery? And then the classroom on-task behavior and the curriculum-aligned learning indicator would be preliminary outcomes. I was going to say they- not evidence of efficacy on their own.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think that framing keeps the inference honest. I’d add the post-program classroom observation as a preliminary durability outcome if the calendar allows, because a within-program change could still be novelty, individual adult attention, or the feedback context itself. The EEG measures can help us characterize mechanism and delivery, but, but they shouldn’t carry the educational claim.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I think that framing works, as long as feasibility includes technical fidelity and not just completed visits. We should count a session as delivered only if the child could tolerate the band and the system actually gave usable feedback for the planned part. Otherwise, we could report a program that looks workable but was not delivered consistently. We can keep the exact signal threshold provisional until I’ve checked the vendor documentation and a few field recordings.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: From the school side, I’d want the proposal to be clear that feasibility means equitable delivery across the four sites, not just a pooled completion rate. I’ll check the assessment and pacing constraints before we lock the preliminary learning measure, but I think we have enough to frame it cautiously for March. I’m just—yeah, I think that’s where we are.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're at time. Thanks, both. Let's reconnect once we've checked the school-calendar and vendor pieces.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Thanks, Maya. Bye, Priya.
